summary: The area's only roadmap, ComputationalNumberTheory (6 stages CN.0–CN.5, proposed, with an integrated decomposition), has 16 findings, none high. CN.4's acceptance treats zero and rank claims as provable by interval enclosures, which exact vanishing cannot be (Cremona §2.13); it needs root-number parity, modular-symbol rationality or Gross–Zagier inputs. CN.4 also plans analytic continuation of cusp-form L-functions, which both libraries already have (Mathlib's `CuspForm.differentiable_Λ`; Tau Ceti's `hasEntireExtension_qExpansion_coeff`), and it lacks edges from ModularForms layer 7 and RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.0. The Boxer–Calegari–Gee items routed to CN.3 need the Miller basis over ℤ and Sturm's congruence theorem, which nothing plans. CN.3 has no edges from Tau Ceti ModularForms, and its Sturm-bound target is already built. The integrated decomposition's RAM-model node is false: RAM steps and bit operations can differ by an unbounded factor (Shoup §3.6). Its nodes also cite no baseline declarations, although several are library results. There are duplications with FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums and with ComplexMultiplicationAndExplicitReciprocity CM.5. PAPER-BENNETT-SIKSEK-20, also routed here, was not examined, because this agent reviewed it.

findings.claim: CN.4's acceptance makes an interval enclosure the certificate for 'zero' and 'rank' claims. An enclosure can certify a sign or nonvanishing, never exact vanishing: an interval containing 0 also contains nonzero values. An analytic-rank claim r has two halves: L^(r)(1) != 0, which an enclosure certifies, and L^(j)(1) = 0 for j < r, which needs an exact argument (root-number parity from the functional equation, exact rationality of L(E,1)/Omega from modular symbols, or Gross-Zagier with Kolyvagin). As written, the clause cannot be met for exact-vanishing claims, and it lets a rank claim rest on the enclosure of one derivative alone. No restructuring touches this clause.
findings.evidence: Roadmap, CN.4: "**Acceptance.** A sign, zero, rank or nonvanishing claim uses an enclosing interval excluding the wrong value; numerical near-equality is not an exact identity." Source: J. E. Cremona, Algorithms for Modular Elliptic Curves (2nd ed.), Section 2.13 'Computing L^(r)(f,1)', printed p. 44 (author's full text https://johncremona.github.io/book/fulltext/chapter2.pdf, read 2026-09-24): "In higher rank cases we have the problem of deciding whether L(k)(f;1) = 0, since no approximate calculation can by itself determine this. ... one finds that L'(f;1) = 0 to 13 decimal places ...; then it is possible to conclude that L'(f;1) = 0 exactly, by applying the theorem of Gross and Zagier"; on the same page the parity of r comes from the W_N-eigenvalue, and whether L(f,1) = 0 "can be determined algebraically". Buhler-Gross-Zagier, Math. Comp. 44 (1985) 473-481, DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1985-0777279-X, abstract: "Assuming the Weil-Taniyama conjecture for this curve, we show that its L-series L(s) has a triple zero at s = 1". Atlas owners of the exact inputs: RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.0 ("Prove the root-number parity relation for the analytic order"), RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.5 ("use modular-symbol rationality at rank zero and the Gross-Zagier/period/index comparison at rank one"), GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights GZ.0-9.
findings.fix: Rewrite CN.4's acceptance: 'A sign or nonvanishing claim (including L^(r)(1) != 0, and the existence of a zero located by a sign change of a real-valued function) is certified by an enclosure that excludes the wrong value. An exact-vanishing claim (L^(j)(1) = 0, hence any lower bound on an analytic rank) is never certified numerically; it is imported from root-number parity (RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.0), exact modular-symbol rationality of L(E,1)/Omega (RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.5), or Gross-Zagier and Kolyvagin (GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights, BSD.5). An analytic-rank certificate is the pair: exact vanishing below r and an enclosure of the r-th derivative excluding 0.' Add the link RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.0 -> ComputationalNumberTheory:CN.4 (CN.4 does not reach BSD.0, so it is acyclic), or else drop 'rank' from CN.4 and state that rank certificates are assembled in RankZeroOneBSD from CN.4's enclosures.

findings.claim: The five BCG items routed to CN.3 need two results that no layer plans and neither library has. (i) The integral structure of level-one forms: V. Miller's basis of S_k(SL2(Z)) with integer q-expansions, so that the matrix of T_p has integer entries and det(T_p | S_k) can be reduced mod p. (ii) Sturm's congruence theorem: a form with coefficients in O that vanishes mod a prime m up to km/12 is 0 mod m. This is what turns a finite check into the congruences a_l(g) = l^25 a_l(f) mod p behind 'rho_f ≅ eps^-25 rho_g'. CN.3's only Sturm target is the characteristic-zero equality bound, which is built. AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights:R15.2 plans abstract integrality of Hecke eigenvalues via Katz's integral q-expansion principle, which gives no explicit integral basis to compute with. The companion-form check recorded in the extraction (a common root of twisted T_2 and T_3 characteristic polynomials mod 107) is evidence, not a certificate.

findings.claim: CN.2's targets (integral bases, orders, ideal decomposition, local expansions) need the key theorems of the standard algorithms at primes that divide the index. The first is p-maximal enlargement (Pohst-Zassenhaus, 'Round 2'): the ring of multipliers of the p-radical strictly contains the order unless the order is p-maximal. The second is Ore's theorem on Newton polygons: the p-adic factorization and prime decomposition read off Newton polygons and residual polynomials, with Montes' higher-order version. No layer plans either. NumberFieldArithmetic layer 3 stops at Dedekind's criterion and Kummer-Dedekind away from the conductor, and its layer 8 states that at a common index divisor no milestone gives the factorization. Neither library has Newton polygons or p-maximal orders; Tau Ceti's only index criterion is the squarefree-mod-p case, and Mathlib has only the discriminant and Eisenstein special steps.

findings.claim: As corrected in review, the acceptance says that in Shoup's RAM model a RAM step count and a bit-operation count agree up to constant factors, and that the magnitude restriction rules out an unbounded factor. That is false. The restriction still allows cells holding numbers of O(len(n+t)) bits, operated on at unit cost, so RAM time and bit complexity can differ by an unbounded, polylogarithmic factor. Shoup says so himself in Section 3.6 with the base-B example. The draft statement that the review 'corrected' was right.
findings.evidence: Node acceptance: "Under this convention a RAM step count and a bit-operation count agree up to constant factors (B is a constant). A cost that allows arbitrarily large integers in single cells is outside the model. [Corrected in review: the draft said bit operations and unit-cost steps differ by an unbounded factor in this model, which the magnitude restriction rules out.]" Shoup v2, Section 3.6 Notes, printed p. 72 (PDF p. 90; same file and hash as the packet's source): "the RAM model, as we formally defined it, invites a certain kind of “cheating,” as it allows one to stuff O(len(ℓ))-bit integers into memory cells. For example, even with the simple, quadratic-time algorithms for integer arithmetic discussed in §3.3, we can choose the base B to have len(ℓ) bits, in which case these algorithms would run in time O((ℓ/ len(ℓ))2). However, just to keep things simple, we have chosen to view B as a constant". Section 3.2, printed p. 55, bounds stored numbers only polynomially: "all numbers stored in memory are at most a′n^b′ + c′ in absolute value".
findings.fix: Replace the item by: 'Check that a claimed running time is a RAM running time in the sense of Shoup Section 3.2: unit cost per instruction, stored numbers at most a′(n+t)^b′ + c′, integers as base-B digit vectors with B a constant. A RAM bound becomes a bit-operation bound only after multiplying by the cost of the word operations the algorithm performs on its O(len(n+t))-bit indices and counters. The two measures can differ by a factor polylogarithmic in the input size (Shoup Section 3.6, p. 72).' Delete the bracketed review remark, and make the hypotheses item say that len(n)-costs are RAM costs, not bit costs.

findings.claim: The node plans Shoup's Theorem 10.2 and the Carmichael test from scratch and cites no library. Mathlib at the pin has the Carmichael predicate (for n > 2 equivalent to Shoup's 'odd composite n with L_n = Z_n^*', oddness being a theorem), squarefreeness (the p_i are distinct), p - 1 | n - 1, Korselt's criterion in both directions, and 561 as a Carmichael number. The Fermat test itself is Nat.ProbablePrime with its ZMod form, and the prime case of Theorem 10.1 is Fermat's little theorem in ZMod p. Only 'r >= 3' is missing. Strong pseudoprimes, L'_n and Theorem 10.3 are absent from both libraries.
findings.evidence: Node statement: "(Theorem 10.2) Every Carmichael number (an odd composite n with L_n = Z_n^*) has the form n = p_1 ... p_r with the p_i distinct primes, r >= 3, and (p_i - 1) | (n - 1)." Acceptance: "Carmichael test: n = 561 = 3 . 11 . 17 satisfies L_n = Z_n^*". Mathlib 082e2d3 Mathlib/NumberTheory/CarmichaelNumber.lean:46 `def IsCarmichael (n : ℕ) : Prop := 2 < n ∧ ¬ n.Prime ∧ ∀ b, b.Coprime n → ProbablePrime n b`; :85 `theorem IsCarmichael.odd`; :97 `theorem IsCarmichael.squarefree (h : n.IsCarmichael) : Squarefree n`; :118 `theorem IsCarmichael.prime_sub_one_dvd {p : ℕ} (h : n.IsCarmichael) (hp : p.Prime) (hpn : p ∣ n) : p - 1 ∣ n - 1`; :127 `theorem isCarmichael_iff_korselt : n.IsCarmichael ↔ 2 < n ∧ ¬n.Prime ∧ Squarefree n ∧ ∀ p, p.Prime → p ∣ n → p - 1 ∣ n - 1`; :151 `theorem isCarmichael_561`. Mathlib/NumberTheory/FermatPsp.lean:55 `def ProbablePrime (n b : ℕ) : Prop := n ∣ b ^ (n - 1) - 1`, :58 `probablePrime_iff_zmod_one ... : n.ProbablePrime b ↔ (b : ZMod n) ^ (n - 1) = 1`. Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finite/Basic.lean:611 `theorem pow_card_sub_one_eq_one {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0) : a ^ (p - 1) = 1`. Shoup Theorem 10.2, printed p. 308: "Every Carmichael number n is of the form n = p1···pr, where the pi's are distinct primes, r ≥ 3, and (pi − 1) | (n − 1)".
findings.fix: Cite Nat.IsCarmichael, IsCarmichael.odd/squarefree/prime_sub_one_dvd, isCarmichael_iff_korselt, isCarmichael_561, Nat.ProbablePrime, probablePrime_iff_zmod_one and ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one as baseline. Keep as new nodes only: the bridge 'for odd n > 1, Nat.IsCarmichael n iff L_n = (ZMod n)ˣ'; 'a Carmichael number has at least three prime factors' (Shoup's r = 2 argument); L'_n with its membership procedure; Theorem 10.3; and the MR error bound. The 561 acceptance test becomes Nat.isCarmichael_561.

findings.where: ComputationalNumberTheory:CN.1 (Acceptance) and data/decompositions/ComputationalNumberTheory.json gaps 'Primality certificates versus primality tests' and 'Integer factorization has no read source anywhere in EXT-08'
findings.claim: The decomposition's gaps say that primality certificates have no source read and integer factorization has no source, and CN.1's acceptance asks for separate probable-prime and proven-prime result types. The pinned Mathlib already has the mathematical core of all three. It has Lucas's theorem in both directions, which is the soundness and completeness of Pratt certificates; the file's own TODO is the certificate tactic. It has the Fermat 'probable prime' predicate, separate from Nat.Prime. It has a checked factorization certificate: FactorsHelper is a sorted list of primes with product n, identified with primeFactorsList by uniqueness. What is missing is the recursive Pratt certificate type with its checker and soundness induction, Pocklington's N-1 criterion, and certificates for large prime factors: FactorsHelper and norm_num prove primality by trial division, whose kernel proofs overflow beyond about 25 bits.
findings.evidence: Roadmap, CN.1: "**Acceptance.** A factorization output multiplies to the original input; probable prime and proven prime are separate result types." Gap: "Next source action: select a source for Pratt certificates (elementary, from Lucas's converse of Fermat)". Mathlib 082e2d3 Mathlib/NumberTheory/LucasPrimality.lean:39 `theorem lucas_primality (p : ℕ) (a : ZMod p) (ha : a ^ (p - 1) = 1) (hd : ∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → q ∣ p - 1 → a ^ ((p - 1) / q) ≠ 1) : p.Prime`, :57 `reverse_lucas_primality`, :73 `lucas_primality_iff`; module doc: "This test is the basis of the Pratt primality certificate. ## TODO - Write a tactic that uses this theorem to generate Pratt primality certificates". Mathlib/NumberTheory/FermatPsp.lean:55 `Nat.ProbablePrime`. Mathlib/Tactic/Simproc/Factors.lean:29 `def FactorsHelper (n p : ℕ) (l : List ℕ) : Prop := p.Prime → (p :: l).IsChain (· ≤ ·) ∧ (∀ a ∈ l, Nat.Prime a) ∧ l.prod = n`, :64 `FactorsHelper.primeFactorsList_eq`, :161 `simproc Nat.primeFactorsList_ofNat`; Mathlib/Data/Nat/Factors.lean:168 `primeFactorsList_unique`. Mathlib/Tactic/NormNum/Prime.lean module doc: "For numbers larger than 25 bits, the primality proof produced by `norm_num` is an expression that is thousands of levels deep, and the Lean kernel seems to raise a stack overflow". Index search: no Pratt or Pocklington declaration in either library.
findings.fix: In CN.1 cite lucas_primality_iff, Nat.ProbablePrime, FactorsHelper and primeFactorsList_unique as baseline. Plan new nodes only for: the inductive Pratt certificate (n, witness a, factorization of n-1 whose prime factors carry certificates), its Boolean checker, soundness from lucas_primality, completeness from reverse_lucas_primality, and the O(log^2 n) size bound; Pocklington's criterion; and a factorization certificate whose prime factors carry Pratt or Pocklington certificates instead of minFac proofs. Algorithmic integer factoring (Shoup Chapter 15) remains a separate complexity target, not part of the certificate.

findings.claim: CN.5's certificate schema for databases is disconnected from the layers whose outputs are the database records. CN.3 has no consumer at all, and CN.5 has no path from CN.1, CN.2 or CN.3 in either direction: it requires only CN.4, whose only CN prerequisite is CN.0. Yet CN.5's acceptance concerns LMFDB records, that is number fields and modular forms, which are CN.2's and CN.3's certified outputs. In RS-03's pattern, other roadmaps instantiate the generic schema (CN.5 -> FF.5, CN.5 -> ED.6), but CN's own number-field and modular-form layers neither instantiate it nor feed it.
findings.evidence: Extract: CN.3 "consumers": []; CN.5 "requires": ["ComputationalNumberTheory:CN.4"]; CN.4 requires CN.0, AN.4 and (RS) AL.1, CA.3, FF.0. RS-03 links out of CN.5: FF.5 ("Instantiate the generic certificate schema for finite-field application handoffs") and ED.6. Reachability over atlas stageEdges plus accepted data/restructure links: no path CN.3 -> CN.5 and none CN.5 -> CN.3. Roadmap, CN.5: "**Acceptance.** An LMFDB label or CAS result supplies data to verify, not a theorem; every dataset-derived claim includes a reproducible certificate."
findings.fix: Connect them in RS-03's direction: add CN.5 -> CN.2 and CN.5 -> CN.3 ('instantiate the generic certificate schema for number-field and modular-form/elliptic-curve records'); both are acyclic. If CN.5 is instead to check those records itself, add CN.2 -> CN.5 and CN.3 -> CN.5. Either way, state which layer checks LMFDB-derived number-field and modular-form claims.
